mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
Given a patient with hypertension, the candidate will
- list and interpret key clinical findings, including those derived from
- an appropriate assessment technique to correctly diagnose hypertension and its severity,
- an appropriate history aimed at eliciting risk factors (e.g., family history),
- an appropriate physical examination aimed at eliciting evidence of acute and chronic target organ damage and secondary causes, and
- a gestational history for pregnant patients and assessment of fetal well-being;
- list and interpret critical investigations, including
- baseline investigations (e.g., creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis),
- tests for risk factors (e.g., lipids, glucose),
- tests for secondary causes where indicated (e.g., urinary catecholamines, thyrotropin [thyroid-stimulating hormone]),
- imaging studies where indicated (e.g., computed tomography of the head, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, abdominal ultrasonography, echocardiography), and
- tests for end organ damage (e.g., urinalysis, electrocardiography); and
- construct an effective initial management plan, including
- reduction in modifiable risk factors (e.g., sodium reduction, weight loss, smoking cessation),
- antihypertensive medication, taking into consideration concomitant conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, renal disease),
- an antihypertensive medication regimen, taking into consideration individual characteristics (e.g., child, older adult [≥ 65 years], pregnant patient), adherence, and potential for adverse effects,
- parenteral agents for hypertensive emergencies and appropriate titration and monitoring,
- strategies for the prevention of complications,
- consideration of psychosocial aspects of taking lifelong medications (e.g., cost, adherence), and
- collaboration with specialists as indicated (e.g., paediatrics, nephrology, high-risk obstetrics).
mcc_objectives.key_objectives: Given a patient with hypertension, the candidate will diagnose the cause, severity, and complications, and will initiate an appropriate management plan. Particular attention should be paid to other cardiac risk factors, existing target organ damage, and the identification of patients with hypertensive urgencies and emergencies.
mcc_objectives.title: Hypertension

- immediate treatment of urgent conditions (e.g., polymyalgia rheumatica),
- immediate symptomatic and supportive treatment (e.g., anti-inflammatories),
- appropriate referral for more specialized care (e.g., rheumatology, physiotherapy) if indicated, and
- counselling regarding appropriate return to activities.

mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
Given a patient who presents with excessive, irregular, and/or abnormal vaginal bleeding, the candidate will
- list and interpret critical clinical findings, including those based on
- first and foremost, the patient’s hemodynamic stability,
- whether the bleeding is related to pregnancy or not,
- information gathered to determine the underlying cause (e.g., other bleeding, medications) if pregnancy has been ruled out, and
- an appropriate physical examination, including a pelvic examination unless contraindicated (e.g., suspected placenta previa);
- list critical clinical investigations and interpret the results of the investigations, including
- a complete blood count, pregnancy test, and in patients with recent pregnancy, qualitative and quantitative β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) tests,
- determining ovulatory status and ordering clinically indicated diagnostic tests, and
- determining whether a referral for investigation is required;
- construct an effective initial management plan, including
- resuscitating the patient if hemodynamically unstable,
- initiating first-line medical therapy for control of abnormal vaginal bleeding and referring the patient for specialized surgical care as appropriate,
- determining if the patient requires other urgent or specialized care,
- outlining legal responsibilities (e.g., mandatory reporting obligations) if sexual abuse is suspected, and
- recognizing the need for counselling and support in case of sexual abuse.

mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
Given a pregnant patient requiring intrapartum and postpartum care, the candidate will
- list and interpret relevant clinical findings, including
- findings based on an appropriate history and physical examination,
- prelabour rupture of membranes,
- indications and contraindications for induction of labour,
- onset, stage, and progression of labour,
- the ongoing emotional and physical needs of a patient in labour,
- features suggestive of a complicated labour (e.g., prolonged stage of labour, fever, meconium-stained fluid),
- possible causes of a complicated labour (e.g., insufficient contractions, cephalopelvic disproportion, infection),
- risk factors for and features of postpartum fever, hemorrhage, and pain,
- socioeconomic determinants of pregnancy outcome, and
- identification of patients at higher risk for postpartum depression;
- list and interpret relevant investigations, including
- appropriate initial investigations for a patient presenting in labour,
- indications and options for fetal and maternal monitoring in labour (e.g., electronic fetal monitoring, fetal blood sampling), and
- appropriate maternal and fetal investigations to determine the need for Rh immunoglobulin;
- construct an effective initial management plan, including
- reviewing maternal birth plans within a model of shared decision-making, including culturally sensitive care,
- encouraging the involvement of birth partner(s) and of extended social supports if appropriate,
- informing the patient about the need for maternal examination and fetal health surveillance, ensuring consent, privacy, dignity, and comfort,
- assessing maternal knowledge of strategies for coping with pain and discussing options for pain management,
- ensuring appropriate management of each stage of labour, including (list not exhaustive)
- determination as to when clinical intervention should not be offered or advised (e.g., uncomplicated labour),
- indications and options for augmentation and active management of labour,
- use of prophylactic antibiotics to reduce the risk of group B streptococcal disease in the neonate,
- appropriate counselling and support when complications are anticipated or encountered (e.g., prolonged stage of labour, nonreassuring fetal status),
- initial immediate management if there are signs of fetal distress,
- determination as to when surgical intervention (e.g., cesarean delivery, episiotomy) or instrumental birth (e.g., forceps) is indicated, and
- initial management of postpartum complications (e.g., hemorrhage, fever, depression);
- ensuring management of preterm labour and prelabour rupture of membranes;
- determining whether the patient requires specialized care;
- offering appropriate management of mental health symptoms; and
- discussing contraceptive needs during the postpartum period and ongoing.
mcc_objectives.key_objectives: The candidate will be able to provide intrapartum and postpartum care that integrates the best available evidence into a model of shared decision-making that enables women to make informed decisions based on their personal needs.

mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
(list not exhaustive)
Given a patient who requires prenatal care, the candidate will
- understand and apply the principles of informed decision-making and patient-centred care, including culturally sensitive care,
- provide care for preconception counselling (e.g., folic acid supplementation, weight management, smoking cessation),
- establish the desirability of the pregnancy in a patient with suspected or confirmed pregnancy and construct an appropriate initial management plan,
- provide initial and subsequent prenatal care that includes an appropriate history, physical examination, exploration of socioeconomic determinants of pregnancy outcome, counselling, and laboratory investigations, and
- identify risk factors and common prenatal complications (e.g., hypertension, maternal age, intrauterine growth restriction) and construct a plan for both the screening and initial management of these conditions.
The candidate will also
- list and interpret relevant clinical findings, including
- factors that contribute to the estimation of the date of confinement (e.g., last menstrual period, date of positive pregnancy test),
- results of a thorough history, including family, social, maternal health, and obstetrical aspects,
- results of systematic screening for tobacco, alcohol, and substance use or exposure,
- indications warranting referral for therapeutic abortion and counselling,
- use of medications and supplements and the need for appropriate counselling,
- findings necessitating timely counselling regarding prenatal genetic screening, including options, risks, benefits, and possible outcomes,
- risk factors and signs of antenatal and postpartum depression,
- signs of intimate partner violence,
- physiological changes characteristic of pregnancy and determination of whether pregnancy is progressing in an uncomplicated manner (e.g., normal pregnancy symptoms), or if complications are present (e.g., hyperemesis, pain, bleeding),
- monitoring aspects in the second and third trimesters, including
- fetal and maternal progress (e.g., weight gain, blood pressure, fetal heart rate and movement)
- signs and symptoms of preterm labour
- determination of fetal lie and presentation in the third trimester
- signs and symptoms consistent with the onset of labour;
- list relevant investigations and interpret the results of the investigations, including
- appropriate initial diagnostic and screening tests (e.g., complete blood count, blood type, rubella status),
- prenatal genetic screening options (e.g., serum integrated prenatal screen, nuchal translucency),
- current recommendations for ultrasonography in an uncomplicated pregnancy,
- indications and options for additional prenatal fetal surveillance (e.g., fetal movement counting, nonstress test, biophysical profile),
- current recommendations regarding screening for prenatal complications and risk factors, including but not limited to
- hemolytic disease of the newborn (e.g., Rh isoimmunization)
- gestational diabetes
- sexually transmitted infections
- group B Streptococcus,
- construct an effective initial management plan, including
- discussing the patient’s adjustment to pregnancy (e.g., mood, work, stress, family),
- counselling and referral to community resources, including
- prenatal and parenting classes
- nutrition, including micronutrients and vitamins
- substance use or substance use disorder
- lifestyle (e.g., physical activity, sexual activity, travel)
- breastfeeding,
- managing common prenatal presentations and complications (e.g., nausea and vomiting, bleeding, intrauterine growth restriction),
- discussing an appropriate follow-up plan for patients with a positive genetic screening result (e.g., amniocentesis, specialist referral),
- managing post-term pregnancy, and
- referring for additional or specialized care if necessary (e.g., preeclampsia, psychiatric disorders, substance use disorder).
mcc_objectives.key_objectives: Given a patient presenting for prenatal care, the candidate will integrate the best available evidence into a model of shared decision-making, enabling patients to make informed decisions based on their needs in all aspects of preconception, pregnancy and fetal health.
mcc_objectives.title: Prenatal care

- outlining legal responsibilities (e.g., mandatory reporting obligations) if sexual abuse is suspected, and
- recognizing the need for counselling and support in case of sexual abuse.

study_units.structural_rationale: GY.S05's printed title 'Fibroids' (extraction_method BODY_HEADING_CONFIRMATION, HIGH confidence) is body-confirmed but the node's inherited page range (609-612) and T-children (Hormonal Methods, IUD, Emergency Postcoital Contraception) belong to an adjacent 'Contraception' section that TOC extraction merged into the same node. Targeted raw-OCR verification of pdf pages 608-612 (undertaken as a follow-up coverage-gap investigation, not part of the original chapter pass) found: pdf page 608 (TN 'GY14') opens with an unambiguous fibroid-specific clinical section (Definition: 'benign smooth muscle tumour of the uterus'; Epidemiology; Pathogenesis), continuing through fibroid-specific management (GnRH agonists/antagonists, uterine artery embolization, myomectomy, hysterectomy) on pdf page 609 (TN 'GY15'); a body-confirmed 'Contraception' heading then begins mid-page-609, introducing the Hormonal Methods/IUD/EPC content already represented as SU-GY-10. Fibroids is therefore a genuine, separate body section with real clinical content of its own - not a cross-reference and not solely a Contraception mis-extraction - represented here as its own study unit against source node GY.S05, with a page range corrected to pdf 608-609 based on direct raw-OCR verification rather than the node's inherited (Contraception-derived) range. No MCC objective names 'fibroids' or 'leiomyoma' as its own presentation; MCC objective 2 ('Abdominal masses and pelvic masses') explicitly lists 'leiomyoma' among its Gynecologic causal conditions, so this unit is mapped as COMPONENT evidence rather than DIRECT.

mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
Given a patient with a possible nerve injury, the candidate will
- list and interpret critical clinical findings, including those based on
- an occupational history and physical examination that can help determine whether a peripheral nerve injury has occurred in the setting of other trauma, and
- identification of the specific nerve involved, framed within a differential diagnosis that distinguishes a nerve injury from other neurologic disorders (e.g., nontraumatic neuropathies, central lesions), and consideration of vasculitic neuropathy if more than one nerve is affected;
- list the critical investigations and interpret the results of the investigations, including
- tests used to detect the presence of a traumatic peripheral neuropathy, and
- tests to screen for vasculitis;
- construct an effective initial management plan, including listing indications for specialized care.
mcc_objectives.key_objectives: Given a patient with a possible nerve injury, the candidate will confirm the diagnosis, cause, severity, and complications, and initiate an appropriate management plan. mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
Given a patient with a bone or joint injury, the candidate will
- list and interpret critical clinical findings, including those derived from a thorough patient history and physical examination, including
- the mechanism of injury and, when required, exclusion of other immediately life-threatening injuries through targeted examination,
- neurologic and vascular status,
- symptoms and signs suggestive of abuse,
- a history of recurrent falls,
- risks for bone abnormalities and/or increased risk for falls or injury, and
- signs of pathologic fractures;
- list critical investigations and interpret the results of the investigations, including
- appropriate imaging modalities, and
- bone density testing and investigations for causes of osteoporosis if relevant;
- construct an effective initial management plan, including
- determining if splinting or casting is indicated,
- restricting weight bearing if indicated,
- prescribing analgesics and anti-inflammatory medications as required,
- referring to specialized care if necessary, and
- choosing the correct treatment for prevention of fractures, including pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatments;
- provide follow-up care and address
- the duration of immobilization if any,
- returning to work and/or normal activity,
- appropriate referral to other health care professionals as needed (e.g., physiotherapist, occupational therapist),
- complications requiring further treatment or referral (e.g., complex regional pain syndrome, compartment syndrome), and
- factors that will affect recovery from the injury (e.g., living situation, employment, nutrition, substance use disorder, general health).
mcc_objectives.key_objectives: Given a patient with a possible bone or joint injury, the candidate will diagnose the cause, assess the severity of the injury, identify possible complications, and construct an appropriate management plan. The candidate will also recognize circumstances in which the patient may have an increased risk for fracture.
mcc_objectives.title: Bone or joint injury

- initiating appropriate pharmacotherapy (e.g., cholinesterase inhibitors),

- determining whether a referral to specialized services (e.g., occupational therapy, substance use disorder treatment) is required.

- Recognize examples of weight bias and weight stigma in health care settings and society in general; describe the adverse consequences of weight stigma on the accessibility and quality of health services for patients

- Demonstrate an understanding of the barriers to health care by people who have experienced or are experiencing incarceration and work towards reducing those barriers
- Understand the different forms of housing insecurity and follow clinical guidelines for individuals experiencing homelessness
- Provide Support
- Acknowledge and appreciate that individuals have different concepts of health and well-being and support diverse cultural practices related to health
- Support diverse cultural practices around medical treatments (e.g., cancer treatments, blood transfusions) and important life events (e.g., birth, death) and acknowledge the limitations of biomedical models of medicine
- Recognize and respect diverse family structures (e.g., blended families, polyamorous families, extended families, chosen families, children in foster care) and community supports when providing health care
- Practice
- Provide trauma-informed and violence-informed care to everyone, recognizing the pervasiveness of historical, intergenerational, and current trauma, including harms caused by or perpetuated by health care providers
- Assess and address the social and structural determinants of health with appropriate tools (e.g., the Poverty Tool, social prescribing), recognizing that an individual’s ability to engage in their health care may be limited due to their social and health inequities and their resources
- Recognize the shortcomings in clinical algorithms, including those that are based on race, ethnicity, sex, and gender identity
- Demonstrate respect and responsiveness by adapting one’s history taking, counselling, physical examination, investigations, and management and demonstrate sensitivity and respect to the patient’s narrative, abilities, and body while being mindful of power dynamics and one’s own privilege
- Assess and address biases in clinical reasoning resulting in underdiagnosing, over-diagnosing, and misdiagnosing (e.g., premature closure, diagnostic overshadowing)
- Follow available clinical guidelines for refugee and migrant health
- Communicate
- Recognize diverse languages and ways of communicating and adapt as required (e.g., drawing on communication aids [e.g., social stories, communication books, interpreters, American Sign Language])
- Recognize when there are other communication barriers and adapt as required (e.g., including health care navigators, including patient advocates)
- Collaborate
- Engage the patient as an equal partner of the collaborative health care team to better address social inequities; include members of the interprofessional team and individuals that patients identify as members of their health care team
- Understand and describe principles of community engagement (e.g., remuneration, equal partnership, addressing community priorities)
- Recognize incidents of discrimination and microaggressions by faculty members, colleagues, patients, or their family members and know what options would be available to address these (e.g., speaking directly with the perpetrator, reporting the incident to appropriate authorities)

mcc_objectives.enabling_objectives:
Given a patient who is dying, the candidate will
- determine whether the patient has the cognitive capacity to discuss and provide informed consent for end-of-life care; if the patient does not have decision-making capacity, the candidate will determine whether advance provisions have been made for goals of care, including the designation of a substitute decision-maker; and
- develop an appropriate management plan, including
- discussing with the patient or substitute decision-maker the patient’s wishes for their care (e.g., full resuscitation) at the appropriate time,
- using pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic measures for symptom control (e.g., pain, respiratory distress, delirium, agitation) while recognizing appropriate indications, adverse effects, and possible complications,
- providing a compassionate response to any request for MAID and taking appropriate steps to ensure the patient has access to this intervention if they meet the eligibility criteria (e.g., make a referral),
- ensuring a culturally sensitive approach to emotional, physical, and spiritual supports for the patient and their family,
- treating the patient, their family, and significant others with dignity and respect throughout end-of-life care, and
- referring the patient to other professionals as needed.
mcc_objectives.key_objectives: Given a dying patient, the candidate will develop an appropriate goals-of-care plan that optimally controls pain and other symptoms, maintains human dignity, and recognizes the importance of family, social supports, and the varied roles of the health care team. The candidate must know the provisions in Canadian law on medical assistance in dying (MAID), be prepared to discuss them with patients, and respond appropriately to such requests.
